Ball 1 starts in the first (front) position.  It is ejected only if that piston fires next, probability = 1⁄3.

Ball 2 starts in the second position.  If its piston fires (1⁄3) it is ejected; otherwise (2⁄3) it moves to the front, where it is ejected with probability 1⁄3.  Thus P₂(win)=1⁄3+ (2⁄3)(1⁄3)=5⁄9≈0.556.

Any ball that first appears in the third position—such as Ball 3—has this tree:
• 1⁄3: its own piston fires → ejected.
• 1⁄3: front piston fires → it moves to the second position, where its chance to be ejected is 5⁄9.
• 1⁄3: middle piston fires → it jumps to the front, where chance to be ejected is 1⁄3.
So
P₃(win)=1⁄3 + (1⁄3)(5⁄9) + (1⁄3)(1⁄3)=17⁄27≈0.630.

Later balls sometimes enter in the second position (chance about 40 %), reducing their success probability to 5⁄9.  Their overall chance therefore stays below 17⁄27.  Hence Ball 3 enjoys the highest possible probability of being piston-ejected.

Let E1,E2,E3 be the eventual ejection probabilities for a ball that is currently in platform positions 1, 2, 3 respectively.

Position 1: the ball is ejected only if piston 1 fires (probability 1/3); otherwise (probability 2/3) it is simply released and lost.  
⇒ E1 = 1/3.

Position 2: with probability 1/3 piston 2 fires and ejects it; with probability 2/3 one of the other pistons fires and the ball moves to position 1, after which its chance is E1.  
⇒ E2 = (1/3)·1 + (2/3)·E1 = 1/3 + (2/3)(1/3) = 5/9.

Position 3: with probability 1/3 piston 3 fires and ejects it; with probability 1/3 piston 2 fires and the ball jumps to position 1; with probability 1/3 piston 1 fires and the ball slides to position 2.  
⇒ E3 = (1/3)·1 + (1/3)·E1 + (1/3)·E2 = 1/3 + 1/9 + 5/27 = 17/27.

Every ball except the first two enters the platform in position 3, so each of balls 3 through 100 has the same ejection probability 17⁄27 ≈ 0.63, larger than the probabilities for balls 1 (1⁄3) and 2 (5⁄9).  Thus any ball numbered 3–100 is optimal; the smallest such number is 3.

Sort Bob’s three guesses so g₁ ≤ g₂ ≤ g₃.  After seeing the guesses, the host will sort the actual coin counts x₁ ≤ x₂ ≤ x₃ and then adversarially pair them (g₃↔x₁, g₂↔x₂, g₁↔x₃) to minimize Bob’s take.  
Bob therefore always earns at least
 payoff = g₁·1{g₁ ≤ x₃}+g₂·1{g₂ ≤ x₂}+g₃·1{g₃ ≤ x₁}.
For every legal distribution of the 30 coins the smallest box can contain 0, so g₃ can always be nullified.  The middle box can be as small as 6, so the host can also nullify g₂ whenever g₂ > 6.  Bob’s guaranteed winnings therefore collapse to g₁ provided g₁ ≤ x₃ for every legal triple.

Among all 72 legal triples (those satisfying x₁+x₂+x₃=30 with one box exactly 6 more than another and at least one box holding ≥2 coins) the minimum possible maximum x₃ is 12, achieved by (6,12,12).  Hence g₁ may not exceed 12, otherwise the host can give every box fewer than g₁ coins and Bob wins nothing.

Taking g₁=g₂=g₃=12 attains this upper limit.  In the worst‐case distribution with only one box holding ≥12 coins (e.g. 0,6,24), the adversarial pairing still forces the host to pay Bob 12 coins.  No higher guarantee is possible because x₃ can be as low as 12.

Thus Bob’s optimal minimax guarantee is 12 coins, worth $12 000.
Label Bob’s three guesses in non-decreasing order r ≤ q ≤ p.

1.  If r ≥ 13, the host can choose the legal distribution (6, 12, 12).  In that case none of Bob’s guesses is ≤ the number of coins in its (adversarially paired) box, so Bob wins 0.  Hence Bob can never guarantee more than 12 coins.

2.  To see that 12 coins can in fact be guaranteed, let Bob guess (12, 12, 12).
   •  For every legal triple of coin counts, at least one box contains 12 or more coins (the smallest possible maximum coin count is 12, attained by 6, 12, 12).
   •  Because all three guesses equal 12, the host can force at most one successful guess (by pairing two boxes that contain fewer than 12 coins with two of Bob’s guesses), but cannot avoid awarding Bob 12 coins from the remaining box that contains ≥ 12 coins.

Thus Bob can ensure he wins at least 12 coins, and no strategy can guarantee more.

Each coin is worth $1 000, so the least amount of money Bob is certain to win is 12 × 1 000 = 12 000.
